checks.name: no-awr machine: install button downloads, verifies, unpacks, binds, continues; failed download changes nothing
checks.details: npm test at 0187633: 393 tests, 390 pass, 0 fail, 3 skipped (lab-dependent). test/awr-install.test.js exercises lib/awr-install.js end to end against a fixture release: a real .tgz (system tar) holding a shell-script awr, a manifest carrying the asset's sha256 (the release-manifest.json artifacts map plays the role criterion 1 calls SHA256SUMS; criterion 3 names the manifest as the source), and a fake fetch. The happy path downloads, verifies the checksum, unpacks into the plugin's state directory, smoke-tests by really starting the binary, and writes current.json only after the smoke test passes. bindProject writes .awr/runtime-binding.json with cli, cli_sha256 and program_version, and a createAwr with an empty PATH resolves the project through that binding ('binding' source) and runs commands, so the takeover continues with the bundled awr and no PATH change. The checksum-mismatch test shows the download is deleted, no current.json and no version directory remain; the client test 'a machine without awr is offered the bundled awr' shows the takeover card replaces its retry with 'Install awr and continue' (no PATH edit anywhere), sends /awr runtime install --use, and the panel then shows the takeover running. Not covered: a physical Windows machine; Windows is exercised only through the win32-x64 target mapping and the tar.exe unpack path in code review, and the takeover continuation is asserted in the client harness, not the desktop app.
criteria:
1. On a machine with no awr on PATH, the takeover panel offers an Install button; accepting downloads the platform release asset, verifies it against SHA256SUMS, unpacks it under the plugin's data directory, writes .awr/runtime-binding.json for the project, and the takeover continues with that awr without any PATH change; a refused or failed download changes nothing on the machine.
2. When the machine already has an awr the plugin can use (capabilities negotiate), that awr is used and no download happens; when the machine awr is too old for a feature, the feature's UI offers the bundled awr instead of stopping.
3. The panel shows the bundled awr's version next to the machine's, a Check asks originoneai/awr releases for a newer one via release-manifest.json, and Update replaces the bundled copy after checksum verification, rolling back to the previous copy if the new one fails to start.

checks.name: compatible machine awr is used unchanged; too-old machine awr gets the bundled-awr offer in the feature UI
checks.details: test/awr-runtime.test.js: with an awr on PATH the resolver keeps source 'path' and the bundled fallback is never consulted (the bundled fake's call log stays empty for that project); binding and DSH_AWR_CLI likewise outrank it, and the bundled copy is used only when nothing else exists ('bundled' source). No code path downloads anything unless the user runs /awr runtime install. For the too-old case, test/client-page.test.js shows the Progress tab's 'awr needs an update' empty state now carries the installer payload (host: lib/progress.js attaches installer.describe() when overview snapshot is unsupported) and offers 'Install awr 0.7.0 to draw the progress' / 'Use the bundled awr 0.7.0'; clicking sends /awr runtime install --use and the page redraws. test/client.test.js shows the bundled-awr line renders beside the machine awr's facts on the card. Not covered: negotiation against a physical old awr binary; the too-old gate is the existing overview-snapshot capability check, unchanged by this work.

checks.name: panel shows bundled version; Check via release-manifest.json; Update verifies checksum and rolls back
checks.details: The card's awr line (client/40-popover.js RuntimeLine) shows 'awr <version>' from installer.describe() while the machine's awr stays in the technical details; the client test asserts the line and the check/apply buttons. Check calls /awr runtime check, which fetches the latest release-manifest.json of originoneai/awr (test asserts the exact URL) and compares versions. Update runs install(): the update test installs 0.8.0 over 0.7.0, asserts current.json.previous points at the old copy whose directory is kept (rollback target and for projects bound to it), and that a third install prunes the oldest; the rollback test installs a release whose binary refuses to start and asserts current.json is byte-identical to before and the failed directory is removed; checksum verification precedes activation (mismatch test). Not covered: an actual GitHub outage during a user's update; failure paths are exercised with the fake fetch returning 404 and corrupted bytes.
